bearerAuth.description: Access token from POST /api/v1/auth/login, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. Lifetime is 15 minutes; refresh through POST /api/v1/auth/refresh, which reads its rotating token from an httpOnly cookie rather than this header.

get.description: Cancellations and expiries are reported separately and deliberately never merged before the caller sees them: a cancellation is a decision the customer made, an expiry is a payment that failed, and they are different problems — `total` is offered so no caller has to add the two, not so anyone has to choose between them. A day with no row is omitted, not zero-filled. `from` and `to` are both required and inclusive, and the range covers at most 366 days.
get.summary: Daily churn, canceled and expired kept apart

get.description: One point per recorded day: total, active, suspended, provisioning, and new gyms. A day with no row is omitted, not zero-filled — see the endpoint group's remarks. `from` and `to` are both required and inclusive, and the range covers at most 366 days.
get.summary: Daily gym counts, recorded days only

get.description: One point per day the nightly job actually recorded, each carrying MRR per currency — amounts in different currencies are never summed or converted. A day with no row is omitted, not zero-filled: a missing day drawn as zero reads as "we lost every gym that night", which a gap does not. `from` and `to` are both required and inclusive, and the range covers at most 366 days.
get.summary: Daily MRR, recorded days only

get.description: Newest first. `action` matches by prefix, so `user.` returns every action on users. Filter by acting user, entity, or time range. Sensitive values are masked at write time and never present to be returned.
get.summary: Search the audit trail

get.description: `from` and `to` are required, inclusive, and at most 366 days apart. Same filters as the list, no paging; rows stream oldest first. Nine columns; `oldValues`/`newValues` are not exported — read them per entry. The export itself is recorded in the audit log with the filter and the row count.
get.summary: Stream the audit trail as CSV

get.description: `oldValues` and `newValues` are JSON objects of the properties that changed.
get.summary: One entry with its before/after values

post.description: Requires the current password. Rotates the security stamp and revokes every refresh token, including the caller's — the client must sign in again. Wrong current passwords count towards the account lockout and are audited, and the endpoint is rate-limited per client IP.

Returns a short-lived access token in the body and sets the rotating refresh token as an httpOnly cookie. Rate-limited per client IP; repeated failures lock the account for the configured lockout period.
post.summary: Sign in with email and password

post.description: Idempotent: succeeds whether or not a valid refresh cookie was presented.

get.description: The single source the frontend gates its UI from. Permissions here are advisory for display only — the API enforces them independently on every call.
get.summary: The signed-in user and their effective permissions

post.description: Rotates the refresh token: the presented token is revoked and replaced. Presenting an already-rotated token is treated as a leak and revokes the rest of that rotation chain.
post.summary: Exchange the refresh cookie for a new access token

get.description: Lets the console show "this link has expired, ask for another" instead of a form that fails on submit. Answers **validity and nothing else** — no email, no name, no roles — so holding a token reveals nothing about the account behind it. Every failure (unknown, expired, already used, account gone or suspended) returns the same `404` with the same `auth.link_not_usable` body, deliberately: a distinct "expired" would confirm the token had once been real.
get.summary: Is this activation link still usable?

post.description: Consumes the link — it works once, and is spent even when the password is rejected by policy, so a refused attempt cannot leave a replayable link behind. Activates a PendingActivation account, rotates the security stamp, and revokes every existing refresh token: a reset ends any session that was already open, which is the point when the reason for resetting is that somebody else is in.
post.summary: Set a password from an invitation or reset link

get.description: The newest audit entries, in a shape sized for a feed rather than the full audit surface. Gated on `audit.read`, not `analytics.read` — this is the audit log wearing a different hat, and audit access must not depend on analytics access, or the reverse. `limit` defaults to 20 and is clamped between 1 and 100.
get.summary: The audit log, trimmed, for the dashboard's activity feed

get.description: The same checks `/health/ready` runs, projected to each check's name and status only. No exception details and no descriptions — either can carry a connection string or a stack trace, and this endpoint is for a status panel, not a debugger.
get.summary: The platform's health checks, for a console panel

get.description: Gym counts and MRR, computed from the operational tables at request time — not from AD-8's daily read model. A summary served from yesterday's row would not be a trade-off, it would be wrong. `mrr` carries one entry per currency; amounts in different currencies are never summed or converted (AD-43 is undecided).
get.summary: The dashboard's headline numbers, live

get.description: Every feature the platform can switch on, with `adoptionCount` — how many gyms currently resolve it **on** through the full three-layer rule (override → plan → platform default), not merely how many plans include it. `overrideCount` is how many of those gyms hold an explicit exception. Both counts exclude deleted gyms, so they describe one population. Ordered by category then name; the catalogue is seeded, so this list is not paged.
get.summary: The feature catalogue

put.description: The **key is not editable** — code branches on it, and it is what the API returns. `If-Match` is **required**: this overwrites what you read, and changing `defaultEnabled` re-answers the feature for every gym that has neither an override nor a plan opinion — the widest blast radius of any write here. `isPremium` is informational: what a gym gets is decided by its plan and its overrides. `adoptionCount` and `overrideCount` are **null** in this response: they are a `GET /features` concern, computed there by a scan this endpoint does not pay for — null means they were not computed for this edit, not that they are zero.

post.description: The gym is created in Provisioning: set up — branding, staff — before members can reach it, then `activate` when it opens. The slug is permanent and is never reused, including by a deleted gym, because it appears in URLs members may still have. Returns the created gym and its `ETag`, so no follow-up GET is needed.

delete.description: Requires the `X-Confirm-Action` header carrying the gym's slug (AD-6): this removes an entire business's access, so a mis-clicked row in a list must not be able to do it. The row survives the retention window so invoices and audit entries stay readable; a purge job performs the hard delete. Terminal — there is no undelete. Repeating the call on an already-deleted gym succeeds. `GET` the gym afterwards to see the recorded deletion.

parameters.description: Step-up confirmation, echoing the resource's own identifier (a gym's slug, an invoice's number). A header rather than a body field so it survives DELETE and cannot be replayed by a script that never read the resource.

Device summary and aggregate stats arrive with the modules that own them (M5–M6) rather than as fields that always read zero.

get.description: The **whole catalogue**, each entry carrying `enabled` and the `source` that decided it — `Override`, `Plan`, or `Default` (§2.4). Not a list of exceptions: "what can this gym do" is the question worth answering, and `source` is what makes the answer explainable in a support conversation. `overrideReason` is present only when an override is what decided it. A gym with no live subscription resolves every feature against the platform default.
get.summary: What this gym's features resolve to, and why

put.description:
An override is stored **only when it differs from what the gym would get anyway**. Ask for exactly what the plan — or the platform default, when the plan is silent — already gives, and any existing exception is **withdrawn** instead, so a gym that later changes plan follows the new plan rather than staying frozen by a row nobody remembers creating. `reason` is therefore required only when an override is actually needed.

The response is the **full resolution, not an echo** of the request: after a withdrawal the stored state is deliberately not what was sent.

Only the keys listed are touched. No `If-Match`: each override is its own record keyed on (gym, feature), so there is no single version to match, and two operators editing different features do not conflict. Deciding what a *plan* includes is `billing.manage` instead.
put.summary: Grant or withdraw this gym's feature exceptions

get.description: Newest first, unpaged — the billing conversation with one gym reads top to bottom. An unknown gym returns an empty list rather than 404: "no invoices" is the truthful answer either way, and the gym endpoints are where a gym's existence is asked about.

get.description: Returns the live subscription — trialing, active, or past due. 404 when the gym has none, which is a normal state: a gym can exist before it is sold anything. The price returned is the one agreed at assignment, not the plan's current price.

put.description:
One operation for both: assigns a subscription when the gym has none, and changes the plan or terms when it does. `billingCycle` and `currency` must match a price the plan actually offers — an absent combination is refused rather than approximated, since guessing would bill an amount nobody agreed to.

A withdrawn plan cannot be newly assigned, though a gym already on one keeps it. The agreed price is **copied**, so later repricing of the plan never changes what this gym pays. Changing plan leaves the paid period alone; charging or crediting the difference is proration, which arrives with invoices in M3.3.

Send `immediately: true` to end it now and forfeit the remainder — a deliberate choice. Ending it now is terminal: a gym that returns gets a new subscription, leaving this one as the record of what it had.

get.description: The overview's `jobs` block on its own, for a page that polls job state. A job is stale when its newest run is still running past one period plus grace, or when it has not succeeded within two periods plus grace (grace is `Monitoring:StaleGrace`, default 5 minutes). A job that has never run is not stale.
get.summary: Every registered job's schedule, last run, next due time and stale flag

get.description: `name` is a registered job, or one that still has history under an old name. `from` and `to` are optional and inclusive on the run's start time; `status` is one of Running, Succeeded, Failed; `limit` <= 0 means the default of 50, and values above 200 are clamped to 200. `hasMore` means older runs exist — page by moving `to` to the oldest `startedAtUtc` returned. A run's `error` is the exception's type and message only; the stack is in the structured log.
get.summary: One job's run history, newest first, paged by time

get.description: Four independently sourced blocks. `health` is the same projection `/dashboard/health` returns. `jobs` lists every registered job, including ones that have never run (`lastRun: null`); `stale` is computed on read from the schedule and the run history. `outbox` is depth only — lag and dead letters arrive with the outbox processor, and `note` says so. `process` is the answering replica's own CPU, memory and uptime, null until its first sample; fleet-wide numbers are App Insights'.

get.description: The features this plan has an **opinion** about (§2.4). A feature absent from the list is not excluded — it is unmentioned, and gyms on this plan fall through to the platform default for it. That third state is why resolution has three layers. Returned as part of the plan, so the response is the plan itself.

put.description: Each entry names a feature `key` and an `isEnabled` of `true`, `false`, or **`null` to clear the plan's opinion** — which makes gyms on the plan fall through to the platform default, a different answer from `false`. Only the keys you send are touched, so a client that knows about ten features cannot erase an eleventh added by a later release. An unknown key rejects the whole request: a half-applied feature set is worse than a refused one. Gated on `billing.manage` because what a plan includes is priced — granting one gym an exception is `features.manage` instead. `If-Match` is **required**.

put.description: Adds the price, or changes it if one already exists for that cycle and currency — one intent, so one operation. Prices are rows, so offering annual billing or a second currency is data entry rather than a schema change. **Existing subscriptions are unaffected**: they hold a price snapshot, so a change applies to new assignments and renewals only. `If-Match` is **required**: this overwrites a price you read, and it is an upsert with no state machine to refuse a stale interleaving, so without it one operator's price silently replaces another's. Returns the updated plan.

Safe for existing subscriptions, which snapshot the price they were assigned. `If-Match` is **required**, like the upsert above: withdrawing a price you may not have seen repriced is the same lost-update hazard from the other direction. Returns the updated plan.

get.description: Every declared setting, optionally narrowed to one `category`. `source` says which layer answered: a stored row beats configuration, which beats the definition's own default. A sensitive key's value comes back as "••••" once a row exists for it — the plaintext is never returned by this endpoint. The Maintenance category is readable here but changes only through its own endpoint, not this one's PUT.

put.description: Every key in `values` must belong to `category`. The Maintenance category is refused here (400 `settings.use_maintenance_endpoint`) — it changes only through its own confirmed endpoint. The whole batch is checked before anything is written: a duplicate key, an unknown key, a key from another category, a value that fails its own rule, or a would-be state that fails cross-field validation all fail the entire batch with nothing changed. Returns the category's fresh views on success.

Returns the Maintenance category's fresh views.
